title: How you travel, and who with
goal: Plan a trip, buy tickets, and say how you're traveling and who with — using the instrumental, the last case you need at A1.
bekal: forming the instrumental and using it for both tools and companions
buying a ticket and understanding basic station announcements

notes: ***Čime?* and *S kim?* are the two instrumental questions.** *Čime ideš?* = how are you getting there? *S kim ideš?* = who are you going with? The answers use the same form: *vozom*, *sa mnom*. You'll use these two questions all the time, and English needs several words for what each of them says in one.

**Tools without a preposition, companions with *s*.** *Idem vozom* (I'm going by train — no preposition) but *Idem s Emirom* (I'm going with Emir). It's a neat, easy-to-remember split: if you **use** the thing, it stands alone; if it **keeps you company**, it gets *s*.

***Sa mnom*, not *s mnom*.** The preposition *s* becomes *sa* before sounds that are hard to join: *sa mnom*, *sa sestrom*, *sa Šejlom*, *sa zetom*. The rule: before *s, š, z, ž*, and before *mnom*. When in doubt, *sa* is always understood.

***Šetat ćemo, jest ćemo*** are the future tense, covered fully in Unit 19. The formula is *ću / ćeš / će…* + dictionary form, with the *-i* of the dictionary form cut off when it comes first. For now, just recognize the pattern.

**Mostar and Stari Most.** An arched stone bridge built by the Ottoman architect Mimar Hayruddin in 1566, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt with stone from the same quarry in 2004. The city's name comes from *mostari* — the bridge keepers. Young men from the city still dive from the top into the Neretva which, as Emir says, is ice-cold all year round.

grammars.title: The instrumental — its forms
body: The fifth and last case you need at A1 (the vocative follows briefly in Unit 20, and it's the easiest of all). There are few endings and almost no surprises.

head: Type
Nominative
Instrumental
Example
rows: **m ending in č, ć, š, ž, đ, dž, j, lj, nj, c**

after: **You already know the plural ending *-ima / -ama*** — it's the same as the dative and locative plural. Three cases, one ending: that's the biggest break Bosnian gives beginners.

**The instrumental has two jobs, and both make sense.** First, **the tool**: *pišem olovkom* (I write with a pen), *idem autobusom* (I go by bus), *jedem kašikom* (I eat with a spoon) — no preposition at all. Second, **the companion**: *idem s bratom*, *razgovaram s Aminom*, *kafa s mlijekom* — with *s* or *sa*.

**The difference matters.** *Idem autom* means I'm going by car. *Idem s autom* means I'm going along with the car — as if it were your walking buddy. Native speakers will smile, but the message won't get through.

**Some verbs always take the instrumental:** *baviti se* (be into, do — *bavim se sportom*), *putovati* (travel by), *služiti se* (use), *postati* (become — *postao je doktorom*), and *razgovarati s* (talk with).

grammars.title: S kim — pronouns and prepositions of place
body: Instrumental pronouns almost always appear with *s* or *sa*, so learn the two together as one chunk.
after: **Five prepositions of place take the instrumental** when they express **a fixed position**: *pod* (under), *nad* (above), *pred* (in front of), *za* (behind), *među* (among). *Ključ je pod stolom.* *Magla je nad gradom.* *Čekam pred kućom.*

**If there's movement toward that place, the case switches to the accusative** — exactly the same pattern as *u* and *na* in Unit 9: *Stavi ključ pod sto* (put the key under the table) vs *Ključ je pod stolom* (the key is under the table).

**A number of time expressions are really frozen instrumentals**, and you've been using them since Unit 12: *ponedjeljkom* (on Mondays), *vikendom* (on weekends), *jutrom* (in the mornings), *noću* (at night), *ljeti* (in summer), *zimi* (in winter), *danima* (for days).

**One expression worth learning whole:** *s dobrom voljom* — with good will, in good spirits. And its equally common partner: *s tobom* in the farewell *Bilo mi je lijepo s tobom* (it was lovely being with you).

blocks.text: Distances in Bosnia are short, but the roads wind between mountains, so travel always takes longer than the map suggests. Sarajevo–Mostar is about 130 kilometers — and still takes two and a half hours, by train or by bus.

head: Bosanski
Say it
English
rows: When does the next train leave?
How long does the trip take?
Where do I get off for the center?

blocks.title: Three words that set trips apart
items: ***Put*** means both road and journey: *Sretan put!* (have a good trip). ***Putovanje*** is travel as an event: *Putovanje traje dva sata.* ***Izlet*** is a day trip with no overnight stay — and it's the word Bosnians use most for weekends like the one in the dialogue.

Trains in Bosnia are few and slow, but the Sarajevo–Mostar line runs through the Neretva canyon and is worth riding once in your life just for the views. For everything else, the bus (*autobus*) is far more frequent and faster.
One lifesaver at the bus station: *Izvinite, ide li ovaj autobus za Mostar?* — excuse me, does this bus go to Mostar?
